Triggers.value: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened
Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try hard to control my emotions
become overly compliant when feeling threatened

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Negative Appraisals.value: My life has been destroyed by the trauma
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.explanation: For a natural-disaster trauma, 'Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents' is a hard-to-explain trigger because it implies a transport/accident trauma context rather than disaster-related cues. This is not just unusual; it mismatches the stated trauma type and is not supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
issues.explanation: The Threat node includes 'Flashbacks', which is more a re-experiencing/memory phenomenon than a current threat belief or arousal cue. Given that Memory is structurally isolated in the formulation, placing a prominent memory-like item in Threat creates a formulation mismatch, especially when no Memory items are endorsed to support that link.

The trigger pattern is difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of natural disaster. 'Being seen' and 'feeling watched or observed' imply an interpersonal/social-threat cue set rather than reminders of an impersonal disaster. With no memory items or appraisals referencing social judgment, persecution, or assault, these two trigger items look clinically mismatched to the trauma context.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed
issues.explanation: The negative appraisals 'I am inadequate' and 'I can't rely on myself' can occur after trauma, but in this profile they pair mainly with social-observation triggers and do not connect clearly to a natural-disaster formulation. The remaining items emphasize generalized threat/hypervigilance, whereas these appraisals suggest a more interpersonal/shame-based presentation. That makes the profile as a whole less coherent.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed
issues.explanation: For a natural-disaster trauma, 'feeling watched or observed' is difficult to reconcile as a trauma-linked trigger. It suggests interpersonal persecution/surveillance rather than an environmental disaster cue, while the other trigger items are disaster-congruent.

issues.item: Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: 'Scanning exits' is not impossible, but paired with a natural-disaster trauma and the other selected items it points toward man-made/interpersonal danger in enclosed spaces rather than the presented disaster context. This makes the threat profile feel partially mismatched to the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate
issues.explanation: The negative-appraisal set is otherwise about global damage and reduced self-reliance after trauma. 'I am inadequate' can occur in PTSD, but here it reads as a generalized self-worth theme without a clear link to the disaster-based trigger/threat pattern, making the appraisal node somewhat less coherent than the other two items.

vignette:
Adaeze Okonkwo is a 21-year-old Nigerian-American woman who, by almost any measure, had built something extraordinary. She had completed her undergraduate degree in three years, earned early admission to a combined MD program, and was, at the time of her trauma, completing a surgical residency rotation - the youngest person in her cohort to do so. She had grown up understanding that excellence was both a gift and an obligation, and she had met that understanding with discipline that impressed even her most demanding attendings. None of that prepared her for the night a tornado tore through the mid-southern city where she was training.

It was late April, and Adaeze had finished a long shift and was walking the three blocks from the hospital to her apartment when the sky turned a particular shade of greenish-grey she had never seen before. The sirens came seconds later. She did not make it inside. The tornado touched down two streets over, and the pressure change was so violent it knocked her off her feet before the debris reached her. She spent what she estimates was forty minutes pinned beneath a collapsed section of wooden fencing and a parked car that had been pushed against it, unable to move her left arm, unable to see anything in the darkness except flashes of lightning, unable to hear anything except the roar and then the terrible silence after. When emergency responders finally reached her, she was certain she was dying. She had not called for help because she had believed, in those forty minutes, that calling out was pointless - that no one was coming, that nothing she did would change what was going to happen to her.

In the weeks that followed, Adaeze returned to her rotation because she did not know what else to do. But the hospital had become a different kind of place. When a trauma case came through the bay - a car accident, a fall, anything that carried the particular charge of sudden bodily catastrophe - her chest would seize and her hands would shake in a way she could not account for clinically. She began arriving earlier and leaving later, telling herself it was professionalism, though she had come to believe that staying busy was the only way to stay in control of something. She stopped running, which had been her primary means of managing stress through medical school; the physical exertion produced a racing heart and shortness of breath that her body no longer distinguished from the moments under that fence. She stopped exercising entirely.

Nights became their own problem. Adaeze would wake in the dark of her apartment and be, for several seconds, completely unable to locate herself in time. The darkness itself had become indistinguishable, in those first moments of waking, from the darkness under the debris. She began sleeping with every light in her apartment on, running up an electricity bill she could not afford on a resident's stipend. When storms rolled through - and in that part of the country they rolled through often - she would monitor the weather radar compulsively for hours before the rain arrived, standing at her window, watching.

She had come to believe, with a quiet and terrible certainty, that what happened to her had exposed something true about the nature of her life: that she had never actually been in control of anything, that the competence she had spent twenty-one years building was a kind of performance that the universe had seen through. She was certain she could not rely on her own judgment. In the operating theatre, she had begun deferring to senior colleagues on decisions she was qualified to make herself, apologising for assessments before she had finished giving them, shrinking in ways that confused the attendings who had previously flagged her as exceptional. She did not experience this as weakness. She experienced it as accuracy - as finally seeing herself clearly.

What brought her to the clinic was a supervising surgeon who had noticed the change and, carefully, suggested she speak with someone. Adaeze had resisted for two months. What finally moved her was a night storm that sent her crouching in her bathroom for three hours, unable to convince herself the walls around her were real. She came to her first appointment exhausted and precise, describing her symptoms the way she would present a case - but what she most feared, she admitted quietly near the end of the session, was that the person she had been before that April night no longer existed, and that no amount of treatment would bring her back.
